title: Information Scent Before Commitment
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Information Scent Before Commitment.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Information scent is the set of cues that helps a person predict where a link, label, result, or control will lead. Strong scent reduces wasted exploration by connecting the person’s current goal and vocabulary to a plausible next destination.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use descriptive labels, useful previews, visible attributes, and consistent terminology. Search results should show why an item matched; navigation labels should name a destination or task; cards should reveal enough consequence to make a choice. Do not over-promise: a label that sounds precise but leads to a broad or unrelated page damages trust.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Treat every link as a prediction
turns.text: What changes when we look at treat every link as a prediction?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Information scent is the set of cues people use to estimate whether a route will move them closer to their goal. Labels, surrounding context, metadata, examples, source, and visual emphasis all contribute. Strong scent is not necessarily verbose; it exposes the distinction that matters for the next choice. Misleading scent can produce fast, confident failure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team tests prediction directly. Participants describe what they expect after selecting a label, what information the destination will contain, and what consequence an action will create. It compares prediction with the actual destination and records confident mismatch.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Analytics can show backtracking or pogo-sticking, but interviews explain whether scent, content, or changed intent caused it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: pricing plans?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A plan name such as “Pro” has weak scent without audience, limits, billing basis, and consequential exclusions. A user should not need to begin checkout to discover that collaboration or data export is unavailable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design predictive cues?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before a person clicks, opens, downloads, starts, or submits, provide enough cue to estimate value and cost. Labels, snippets, metadata, source, format, date, size, eligibility, price, duration, and consequence create scent. The right cues depend on the decision.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Strong scent is distinctive and honest. “Learn more” provides little prediction; “Refund eligibility and deadlines” narrows uncertainty. A card image may attract attention without explaining destination. Avoid clickbait or concealed conditions that create traffic while damaging task success.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test links and results in their surrounding set. Ask people where they expect each route to lead and what information supports the choice. Measure pogo-sticking, rapid backtracking, reformulation, abandonment, and downstream completion. Poor scent can look like navigation failure after the click.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Preserve scent across transitions: destination heading, state, and content should confirm the promise. When a route requires commitment, expose material prerequisites and alternatives beforehand so the person can choose without sunk effort.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at engineer scent across the path?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unknown and negative evidence are part of scent. If step-free access is unverified, omitting the field encourages the optimistic inference that no problem exists. If an option cannot accept a particular referral type, showing it as available and revealing the exclusion later wastes work and may threaten care continuity.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Strong scent can appropriately reduce clicks, because the person avoids an unsuitable route before investing effort.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team tests scent through prediction, first choice, destination confirmation, backtracking, and downstream outcome. Search analytics reveal repeated reformulation; rapid return can indicate weak scent or genuinely comparative behaviour. Interviews and controlled tasks distinguish the mechanisms.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The resulting evidence updates labels, summaries, metadata, ranking, and sometimes the underlying service promise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: cloud pricing?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A “Business” plan card has weak scent if it omits billing basis, collaboration limits, support level, data residency, and the point at which charges grow. Users may enter checkout quickly and abandon later. Exposing decisive differences earlier can lower checkout starts while improving qualified completion and trust.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Stronger scent may reduce conversion by helping people avoid an unsuitable route. Senior practice protects this service value from teams that optimise entry clicks, and treats unknown or adverse evidence as part of an honest pre-commitment experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Two links sit beneath a billing question: “Account services” and “Change payment method.” The first sounds organisational; the second predicts the destination and consequence. The difference is information scent.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before opening three links or product cards, write what you expect behind each. Compare the destination with your prediction and identify which cue created any confident mismatch.
